Under the general Area process, where a student acknowledges responsibility and warning/probation is the likely outcome, the Dean may offer administrative resolution. The student may accept or reject in writing; acceptance is final and unreviewable within the University except if new material information leads to withdrawal and committee referral. This is not an automatic AI penalty.

Under the general Area sanctions framework, only the Area Disciplinary Committee may suspend or expel a student; it may recommend revocation for misconduct before degree conferral. These are possible general sanctions, not fixed AI-use penalties or College-specific procedural deadlines.

Academic units have their own written disciplinary procedures; the central Area page provides a general outline. College students must use the separately published College process and Harris students must check Harris rules. General sanctions do not establish an automatic penalty for AI use.
Within BSD PhD and Master’s programs, students should not rely on generative AI for graded coursework or examinations unless the instructor, program or committee has approved the use in advance.

BSD requires enterprise-approved tools for University data and specifically IRB- or data-agreement-approved tools for regulated research data. Public AI tools may be used only with non-sensitive public information; protected student, personal and unpublished/restricted research data require approval for that use.

AI cannot be an author on BSD-affiliated scholarly products. AI contributions must be disclosed according to the target venue’s requirements, and AI use in human-subjects protocols must be disclosed to the IRB.

BSD thesis/dissertation, capstone and independent-project AI use is subject to mentor, program or committee discretion. Core research, analysis and conclusions must remain the student’s own. Absent specific guidance, use beyond basic language editing requires prior scoped authorization; approved use must be disclosed.
CCRF prohibits materials prepared with generative AI assistance, expressly including Phoenix AI, in its undergraduate research and national fellowships applications.
Whether AI writing and research tools constitute academic dishonesty depends on the instructor of record’s rules. Students should address doubts about appropriate use to that instructor.

The College disciplinary process must not presume credibility or culpability. OCCS or the relevant committee gathers and evaluates information and determines responsibility by a preponderance of evidence. This is a general procedure, not an automatic AI penalty.

College guidance recognises AI detectors are imperfect. Instructors and OCCS may use Pangram as supporting information in a transparent, human-led academic integrity process and student conversations; it is not automatic proof of misconduct. Unit policies and instructor choices may differ.

A College student may request review of a committee decision imposing a sanction after a responsibility finding. Review follows the separately referenced University procedures; no unverified deadline or automatic appeal outcome is inferred here.

Before a College Area Disciplinary Committee meeting, the student receives the written materials and at least two business days to submit a response. This committee-stage rule must not be confused with other stages or academic units.

College students may bring a support person, who may advise but may not speak for the student or question the subcommittee. Students should notify OCCS three to five business days in advance; for a lawyer, notice should be at least seven business days and University counsel must also attend.

Harris requires citation of the specific AI program used. Students should explain how AI was used and save full original generated text in case requested; failure to cite AI use constitutes academic dishonesty.

Harris permits AI coursework assistance only when the course/instructor does not prohibit it, AI supports rather than replaces learning, the specific program is cited and the student checks accuracy. Students should explain use and save original outputs in case requested.

Harris disciplinary probation entails specified restrictions on emergency scholarship funding and Career Development/HarrisLink services, permanent ineligibility for on-campus academic jobs such as TA/proctor, and loss of good standing. Further violations during probation are referred to the Area committee. These are general sanction consequences, not automatic penalties for AI use.
History faculty specify classroom AI policies in the syllabus. In the absence of a syllabus statement, the departmental assumption is that generative AI use in the class is prohibited.
History faculty and instructors will refrain from using generative AI to grade student assignments.
Law School generative AI use is prohibited during exams by default unless the instructor specifies otherwise. The default does not prohibit compliant use while studying for an exam.

Law School §4.9 covers generative and agentic functions, including embedded tools and multi-agent systems. Basic error correction and source search/retrieval are excluded, but substantive rewriting and generated synthesis count as AI.

Under the Law School default, AI use in submitted work is compared to unattributed use of a human author’s work. Some uses such as brainstorming or proofreading can comply; AI composing all or part of a paper violates the default even with attribution.
Law School instructors may set different AI policies. Deviations from the default must be stated in writing in the syllabus posted on Canvas.
PhoenixAI users are responsible for citing generated content used in papers, presentations, course assignments or publications. Service access and citation do not override assessment restrictions.
PhoenixAI is intended for education, research and professional development; commercial use is prohibited.

UChicago reserves the right to monitor PhoenixAI for compliance, subject to its account-privacy policy. Noncompliance may lead to restricted access or other disciplinary action; this does not establish unrestricted monitoring or a fixed AI penalty.

UChicago student guidance states that AI use without proper attribution breaches academic integrity. Its detailed guidance calls for acknowledging AI assistance when appropriate; attribution does not override instructor or unit prohibitions.
UChicago student guidance requires students to follow the instructor’s rules on when and how AI may be used in coursework. Course policies may differ; students should ask when unclear.

UChicago’s general guidance prohibits vendors from training or improving models with University data. The Workspace Studio table separately warns that data may be shared for training unless users opt out. Both statements are retained; automatic activation is not evidence of permission to enable training, and the University’s reconciliation remains unverified.
